Fuel for Petrol Engines
Petrol is a common liquid fuel used for two and four-wheeler light passenger vehicles. It is a mixture of about 150 volatile hydrocarbons with carbon atoms between 4 to 12 per molecule. Petrol contains straight and branched-chain alkanes (paraffins), cyclic alkanes (naphthenes), unsaturated hydrocarbons with one double bond (olefins) and aromatic hydrocarbons, with an average chemical composition of C8.26H15.5.
This problem will explore combustion of petrol and related fuels being used commercially in petrol engines. Some useful data:

| Compound | Density (g cm–3) | ΔH°combustion (kJ mol–1) |
|---|---|---|
| n-octane (l) | 0.70 | ‒ 5470.3 |
| cyclohexane (l) | 0.77 | ‒ 3918.6 |
| isooctane (l) | 0.69 | ‒ 5461.0 |
| ethanol (l) | 0.79 | ‒ 1366.8 |

PART A: Combustion in Petrol Engines
The combustion of petrol can be understood with octane as a model fuel.
1.1 Draw structures of all possible stereoisomer(s) of octane having two chiral centers, in the wedge-dash representation.

The combustion of fuel starts with a homolytic cleavage of a C–H bond in a hydrocarbon, forming alkyl radicals. These radicals can undergo rearrangement to form more stable radicals. If the radicals generated are unstable even after rearrangement, the fuel can burn at low temperatures. Among the alkyl radicals generated by the octane isomers during combustion, those formed by isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) are most stable, some of which are stabilized by rearrangement.
1.2. Draw the structure(s) of all probable alkyl radical(s) that are formed from isooctane including those after rearrangement. Identify the most stable free radical by circling its structure.

In a petrol engine under certain conditions, some components of the fuel-air mixture forming less-stable free radicals may self-ignite without ignition by the primary flame front as shown in the diagram below. Such secondary flames outside the primary flame front create secondary heat and pressure waves. Multiple pressure waves in the cylinder can create shock waves and cause jerky movements of the piston. The shock waves also create a characteristic "pinging" sound, known as knocking. Knocking tendency of a fuel (causing jerky movements in vehicle) is quantified by octane number. The fuel that causes less knocking is considered better and is assigned a higher octane number.

[Diagram description: Two side-by-side diagrams of a petrol engine cylinder. The left diagram, labeled "Smooth combustion", shows a spark plug igniting the fuel mixture, creating a single, smooth "Primary Flame" front that expands downwards towards the piston. The right diagram, labeled "Knocking", shows a similar cylinder where the spark plug ignites a "Primary Flame", but a "Secondary flame front" has spontaneously ignited at the side of the cylinder, separate from the primary flame, creating multiple flame fronts.]

1.3. Arrange the following hydrocarbons in ascending order of their knocking tendency.
methylcyclohexane, isooctane, n-octane, toluene (methylbenzene)

1.4. Estimate the stoichiometric amount of air (in g) required for the complete combustion of 100 cm3 of a liquid fuel mixture containing n-octane and cyclohexane [70:30, v/v assuming volumes are additive]. Write balanced equations for the combustion of each component. Assume composition of air (v/v) at NTP as: Argon (0.95%), Nitrogen (78.08%) & Oxygen (20.95%).

Air-fuel ratio (λ) is the relative stoichiometric ratio between the mass of air and the mass of fuel that are injected in the engine. When λ = 1, the combustion mixture in the engine contains a stoichiometric amount of air and fuel; values of λ < 1 signify fuel-rich mixtures, while λ > 1 correspond to air-rich mixtures. This ratio affects the composition of emitted gases from the engine.

Concentration values of two gases in a petrol engine exhaust as a function of λ are presented as two curves in the graph here.
[Graph description: A line graph showing "Exhaust gas emissions (ppm)" on the y-axis versus "λ" on the x-axis. The x-axis ranges from 0.70 to 1.20. The y-axis ranges from 0.0 to 400.0. There are two unlabeled curves. Curve 1 starts at approximately 250 ppm at λ = 0.72, and steadily decreases as λ increases, reaching approximately 120 ppm at λ = 1.18. Curve 2 starts at approximately 40 ppm at λ = 0.72, increases to a peak of approximately 360 ppm around λ = 1.10, and then decreases to approximately 290 ppm at λ = 1.18.]

1.5. If 20% excess air (λ = 1.2) is injected in a petrol engine for combustion of a fuel mixture containing octane (85% v/v), cyclohexane (5% v/v), 2-butene (5% v/v) and toluene (5% v/v), identify the gases emitted in the exhaust in significant concentrations (above 200 ppm). Mark X for the correct option(s).
a) CO2
b) CO
c) Ar
d) NOx
e) N2
f) O2
g) unburnt hydrocarbons (HC)

PART B: Mixing Ethanol with Isooctane
Most governments have been imposing vehicle emissions regulations that are continually being tightened further. BS VI emission standards notified by the Government of India limit values of exhaust gases for two wheelers fitted with spark ignition engines as follows: CO (500 mg km–1), HC (100 mg km–1), NOx (90 mg km–1).
[Reference: The Emission Standards for Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI), Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, May 2020].

Changing fuel compositions can address some of the emission concerns. Ethanol is one of the alternative transportation fuels which is available as a byproduct from agricultural sources.

1.6. Consider the liquid fuel for an engine is changed from isooctane (F0) to a mixture containing 80% isooctane and 20% ethanol (v/v, assuming volumes are additive), known as F20.
(i) Estimate the difference in calorific values of these two fuels, C (F20) – C (F0), heat released per g.
(ii) By what percent CO2 emission is reduced on changing the fuel from F0 to F20 for the same distance covered by the vehicle? Assume 100% efficient combustion and the efficiency of engines in the two cases to be identical.

PART C: Ethanol Blended Petrol
Ethanol blended petrol in different proportions is being used in different parts of the world including India. E85 is blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol, E20 is 20% ethanol blended with 80% petrol and so on. The ignition temperature of fuel is the temperature at which it spontaneously ignites in atmospheric air without an external source of ignition. Certain facts associated with ethanol blended fuels are:
F1. Ethanol forms an azeotrope with water.
F2. Addition of double bonds to alkyl chain of a fuel mixture stabilizes some of its alkyl radicals.
F3. Ethanol molecules are inherently rich in oxygen.
F4. The ignition temperature of ethanol is 365 °C and that of petrol is 247 - 280 °C.
F5. Ethanol-blended petrol absorbs water from atmosphere.
F6. Oxygen containing fuels inhibit formation of soot.
F7. Latent heat of evaporation of ethanol is much higher than that of octanes.

1.7. State which of the following statements are correct/ incorrect for petrol engines and write the fact/s (F1 - F7) which justify your answer.
S1. The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.
S2. Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.
S3. E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.
S4. E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at λ = 1.
S5. Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.

This is a comprehensive chemistry problem focusing on fuel properties, combustion stoichiometry, and emissions. Below is the step-by-step reasoning and the clear final answers for each part.

### **PART A: Combustion in Petrol Engines**

**1.1 Structures of stereoisomers of octane having two chiral centers**
*   **Reasoning:** $n$-octane has no chiral centers. To satisfy the condition, we must pick an isomer of octane ($C_8H_{18}$) that possesses exactly two chiral centers. A classic example is **3,4-dimethylhexane**. Its carbon backbone is $CH_3-CH_2-C^*H(CH_3)-C^*H(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3$. Carbons 3 and 4 are bonded to four different groups: a methyl, an ethyl, a hydrogen, and the rest of the chain. Because the molecule is symmetric, it yields exactly three stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers and a meso compound.
*   **Answer:**
    *   **(3R, 4R)-3,4-dimethylhexane:**
        ```text
              CH2CH3     CH2CH3
                \         /
        CH3CH2 --- C ------- C --- CH2CH3
                /   \     /   \
               H    CH3 CH3    H
        ```
        *(Note: Top C has H going into page (dashed) and CH3 coming out (wedged); Bottom C is the mirror image of the top).*
    *   **(3S, 4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane:** The exact mirror image of the (3R, 4R) structure.
    *   **meso-(3R, 4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane:** Contains an internal plane of symmetry. Both C3 and C4 have one wedge and one dash that mirror each other, rendering the molecule achiral overall despite having two chiral centers.
        ```text
              CH2CH3     CH2CH3
                \         /
        CH3CH2 --- C ------- C --- CH2CH3
                /   \     /   \
              CH3    H   H    CH3
        ```

**1.2 Probable alkyl radicals from isooctane**
*   **Reasoning:** Isooctane is 2,2,4-trimethylpentane ($CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_3$). Homolytic cleavage of C-H bonds can yield primary, secondary, and rearranged tertiary radicals.
*   **Answer:**
    1.  **Primary radical at C1:** $^\bullet CH_2-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_3$ (Unstable)
    2.  **Secondary radical at C3:** $CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH^\bullet-CH(CH_3)-CH_3$
    3.  **Secondary radical at C4:** $CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-C^\bullet(CH_3)-CH_3$
    4.  **Primary radical at C5:** $CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2^\bullet$
    5.  **Rearranged Tertiary radical at C2:** The highly unstable primary radical at C1 undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to form the **most stable free radical**.
        **[Most Stable Radical]**: $CH_3-C^\bullet(CH_3)-CH_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_3$ *(Tertiary 2,3,4-trimethylpentyl radical)*

**1.3 Ascending order of knocking tendency**
*   **Reasoning:** Knocking tendency is inversely proportional to the octane number (a higher octane number means lower knocking). Isooctane is the standard for 100 octane. n-octane is extremely prone to knocking (~ -10 octane number). Methylcyclohexane is moderate (~75). Toluene has excellent anti-knock properties (~120).
*   **Answer:** **Toluene < Isooctane < Methylcyclohexane < n-octane**

**1.4 Stoichiometric amount of air for 100 cm³ of fuel mixture**
*   **Reasoning:**
    *   **Volumes & Masses:** 70 cm³ n-octane ($70 \times 0.70 = 49$ g); 30 cm³ cyclohexane ($30 \times 0.77 = 23.1$ g).
    *   **Moles:** n-octane ($C_8H_{18}$, M=114.23 g/mol) $\rightarrow 49 / 114.23 = 0.429$ mol. Cyclohexane ($C_6H_{12}$, M=84.16 g/mol) $\rightarrow 23.1 / 84.16 = 0.274$ mol.
    *   **Balanced Equations:**
        $C_8H_{18}(l) + 12.5 O_2(g) \rightarrow 8 CO_2(g) + 9 H_2O(g)$
        $C_6H_{12}(l) + 9 O_2(g) \rightarrow 6 CO_2(g) + 6 H_2O(g)$
    *   **$O_2$ Required:** $(0.429 \text{ mol} \times 12.5) + (0.274 \text{ mol} \times 9) = 5.3625 + 2.466 = 7.8285$ mol $O_2$.
    *   **Air Required:** Air is 20.95% $O_2$ by volume (and mole). Moles of air = $7.8285 / 0.2095 = 37.367$ mol.
    *   **Average Molar Mass of Air:** $(0.7808 \times 28.01) + (0.2095 \times 32.00) + (0.0095 \times 39.95) = 28.95$ g/mol.
    *   **Mass of Air:** $37.367 \text{ mol} \times 28.95 \text{ g/mol} = 1081.8$ g.
*   **Answer:** **~1082 g**

**1.5 Exhaust gases > 200 ppm at $\lambda = 1.2$**
*   **Reasoning:** $\lambda = 1.2$ means 20% excess air. The combustion is highly efficient, making CO and unburnt HC negligible. The exhaust will be primarily composed of bulk air components that do not react ($N_2$, $O_2$, Ar) and the primary combustion product ($CO_2$). Furthermore, peak $NO_x$ emissions occur at slightly lean air-fuel mixtures (like $\lambda = 1.1$ to $1.2$). As seen in the text graph, at $\lambda \approx 1.18$, the $NO_x$ curve sits at ~290 ppm. 
*   **Answer:** Mark **X** for:
    *   **[X]** a) CO2
    *   **[ ]** b) CO
    *   **[X]** c) Ar
    *   **[X]** d) NOx
    *   **[X]** e) N2
    *   **[X]** f) O2
    *   **[ ]** g) unburnt hydrocarbons (HC)

---

### **PART B: Mixing Ethanol with Isooctane**

**1.6 Fuel change from F0 to F20**
*   **Reasoning:**
    *   **Calorific Values (per gram):**
        *   **F0 (Isooctane):** 100 cm³ $\times$ 0.69 g/cm³ = 69 g. Moles = $69 / 114.23 = 0.6040$ mol. Heat = $0.6040 \times 5461.0 \text{ kJ/mol} = 3298.6 \text{ kJ}$. $C(F0) = 3298.6 / 69 = \mathbf{47.81 \text{ kJ/g}}$.
        *   **F20 (80/20 blend):** 80 cm³ isooctane ($80 \times 0.69 = 55.2$ g) + 20 cm³ ethanol ($20 \times 0.79 = 15.8$ g) = 71 g total. 
            Heat from isooctane = $(55.2 / 114.23) \times 5461.0 = 2638.9 \text{ kJ}$. 
            Heat from ethanol = $(15.8 / 46.07) \times 1366.8 = 468.8 \text{ kJ}$. 
            Total Heat = $3107.7 \text{ kJ}$. $C(F20) = 3107.7 / 71 = \mathbf{43.77 \text{ kJ/g}}$.
    *   **$CO_2$ Emissions:**
        To cover the same distance with identical engine efficiencies, the engine must extract the *same total amount of heat energy* (let's call it $Q$) from either fuel.
        $CO_2$ produced per kJ for F0: $(8 \text{ mol } CO_2 \times 44.01 \text{ g/mol}) / 5461.0 \text{ kJ} = \mathbf{0.06449 \text{ g } CO_2/\text{kJ}}$.
        $CO_2$ produced per kJ for F20: [((55.2/114.23)*8 + (15.8/46.07)*2) * 44.01] / 3107.7 kJ = $200.32 / 3107.7 = \mathbf{0.06446 \text{ g } CO_2/\text{kJ}}$.
*   **Answer:**
    *   (i) Difference in calorific values: $C(F20) - C(F0) = 43.77 - 47.81 =$ **-4.04 kJ/g**.
    *   (ii) $CO_2$ emission is reduced by essentially **0%** (specifically a ~0.046% reduction). Both fuels produce nearly the exact same mass of $CO_2$ per unit of energy released.

---

### **PART C: Ethanol Blended Petrol**

**1.7 Evaluation of Statements**
*   **S1. The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.**
    *   **Correct.** Justification: **F4** (The much higher ignition temperature of ethanol compared to petrol means it is far more resistant to spontaneous combustion/ignition, raising the octane number and lowering knocking).
*   **S2. Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.**
    *   **Correct.** Justification: **F7** (Ethanol absorbs significantly more heat to evaporate. This strong "charge cooling" effect brings the temperature of the air-fuel mixture down drastically in E85).
*   **S3. E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.**
    *   **Correct.** Justification: **F1, F5** (Because ethanol absorbs atmospheric water and forms an azeotrope with it, the fuel mixture becomes acidic/corrosive, which damages metallic engine parts, lines, and seals if not properly modified).
*   **S4. E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at $\lambda = 1$.**
    *   **Incorrect.** Justification: **F3, F6** (Ethanol molecules contain oxygen. Oxygen-containing fuels promote more complete combustion, thus *decreasing* unburnt hydrocarbon emissions).
*   **S5. Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.**
    *   **Incorrect.** Justification: **F6** (Oxygenates inhibit the formation of soot. Because soot makes up particulate matter, PM emissions would be decreased, not increased).

PET has repeating unit [-O-C(=O)-C6H4-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-]n.

Part A. PET
2.1 A PET sample is heated with excess aqueous base, cleaving the ester bonds completely.
(i) Name or write the products.
(ii) From the resulting mixture, choose a sequence from the following processes to isolate the two monomers that can remake PET. For each chosen step, state the mixture being treated and the compound separated.
Processes: I filtration; II reduced-pressure distillation near 100 C; III extraction with toluene; IV treatment with aqueous sodium bicarbonate; V addition of water; VI treatment with iodine; VII acidification; VIII normal-pressure distillation near 100 C; IX heating under inert gas.

2.2 PET is treated with an unknown liquid B (3n equivalents) and a Lewis-acid-type acetate catalyst to give bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate, HO-CH2-CH2-O-C(=O)-C6H4-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-OH.
(i) Identify B.
(ii) Choose the catalyst role: (a) Lewis acid catalyst, (b) dehydrating agent, (c) acetylating reagent, (d) Bronsted base catalyst.
(iii) Classify the reaction: (a) elimination, (b) addition, (c) nucleophilic substitution/transesterification, (d) electrophilic substitution.

2.3 PET is treated with excess 2-aminoethanol and a zinc acetate catalyst. Give the products after complete reaction.

2.4 Which depolymerization route can obtain PET back with the least chemical waste/byproduct and least energy input: (a) water hydrolysis, (b) base hydrolysis, (c) treatment with B and the acetate catalyst, or (d) treatment with 2-aminoethanol and zinc acetate?

Part B. Polythene
Mechanical stress in air can introduce carbonyl-containing groups into some polyethylene chains. The original sheet is clear; the mechanically stressed sheet is cloudy/wrinkled.

2.5 Give generic species X, Y, and Z in an autoxidation scheme where oxygen reacts with a polymer radical to form a peroxy species and ultimately oxygen-containing chain products.

2.6 Choose the statements that can explain reduced transparency: (a) scattering from roughness/defects, (b) PET hydrolysis, (c) no chemical change is possible, (d) crystalline/defect domains scatter light.

2.7 Choose reasonable limitations for mechanical recycling: (a) lower purity worsens quality, (b) repeated processing can degrade chains, (c) it always returns pure monomer, (d) no sorting is needed.

2.8 Mark whether each limitation belongs to mechanical or chemical recycling: (a) sensitive to purity/degradation; (b) requires chemical reagents/separation; (c) product properties decline after repeated cycles.

Return concise numbered answers for all subparts.

# Problem 3: CaO Production

---

## 3.1 — Balanced Equations for CaCO₃ Preparation

$$\text{Step 1: } \text{CaO(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(s)}$$

$$\text{Step 2: } \text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

---

## 3.2 — Calculating K_c at 835 °C

For the heterogeneous equilibrium CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), only CO₂ appears in the equilibrium expression.

$$K_p = P_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.236 \text{ atm}$$

$$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}, \quad \Delta n = 1$$

$$K_c = \frac{K_p}{RT} = \frac{0.236}{0.08205 \times 1108.15} = \frac{0.236}{90.92}$$

$$\boxed{K_c \approx 2.60 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}}$$

---

## 3.3 — Thermodynamic Calculations

**First, determine ΔH° and ΔS° for Reaction 1:**

$$\Delta H^\circ = \Delta H^\circ_f(\text{CaO}) + \Delta H^\circ_f(\text{CO}_2) - \Delta H^\circ_f(\text{CaCO}_3)$$
$$= (-635.6) + (-393.5) - (-1206.9) = +177.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S^\circ = S^\circ(\text{CaO}) + S^\circ(\text{CO}_2) - S^\circ(\text{CaCO}_3)$$
$$= 39.8 + 213.6 - 92.9 = +160.5 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} = 0.1605 \text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$

### (i) Standard Free Energy at 25 °C and 850 °C

**At 25 °C (298.15 K):**
$$\Delta G^\circ = 177.8 - 298.15 \times 0.1605 = 177.8 - 47.9 = \boxed{+129.9 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

**At 850 °C (1123.15 K):**
$$\Delta G^\circ = 177.8 - 1123.15 \times 0.1605 = 177.8 - 180.3 = \boxed{-2.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

### (ii) Temperature Below Which Decomution Does Not Occur (P_CO₂ = 1 atm)

For spontaneity when P(CO₂) = 1 atm: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln(1) = ΔG° < 0

$$T > \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{\Delta S^\circ} = \frac{177.8}{0.1605} = 1107.8 \text{ K} \approx 835 \text{ °C}$$

$$\boxed{T < 1108 \text{ K } (835 \text{ °C})}$$

Below this temperature, CaCO₃ will **not** spontaneously decompose when P(CO₂) = 1 atm.

## 3.4 — Le Chatelier Modifications

CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)  ΔH° = +177.8 kJ/mol (endothermic)

| Modification | Observed change(s) |
|---|---|
| 1] Temperature increased | **A, B** — Endothermic reaction shifts right; more CaO and CO₂ |
| 2] Volume doubled (40 L) | **A, B** — P(CO₂) drops below Kₚ; equilibrium shifts right to restore Kₚ, requiring more moles of CO₂ in the larger volume |
| 3] Half CaCO₃ removed | **C** — Activity of a solid = 1 as long as some solid remains; equilibrium unchanged |
| 4] Finely powdered CaCO₃ | **C** — Particle size affects rate, not equilibrium position (activity of solid is independent of surface area) |

---

## 3.5 — Furnace Temperature Comparison

$$\boxed{T(\text{Zone 3}) \;<\; T(\text{Zone 4})}$$

**Supporting reason: (b) Positive ΔH of reaction 1** ✓

The endothermic decomposition (ΔH° = +177.8 kJ/mol) requires substantial heat input. Zone 4, where the fuel flame directly provides this energy, is the hottest zone. Zone 3 (preheating zone) receives heat only indirectly from rising gases and is therefore cooler.

## 3.6 — Zone Identification

| Description | Zone |
|---|---|
| A) CO₂ pressure is lowest | **Zone 5** — Fresh air enters at the bottom with essentially zero CO₂; no decomposition occurs below Zone 4 |

| C) Maximum percent conversion of CaCO₃ | **Zone 4** — Direct flame heating drives the endothermic decomposition most rapidly here |
| D) Solid has maximum % of CaO | **Zone 5** — All CaCO₃ has already decomposed in Zone 4; the solid exiting at the bottom is essentially pure CaO |
| E) Gaseous mixture has highest pressure | **Zone 4** — Both fuel combustion (→ CO₂ + H₂O) and CaCO₃ decomposition (→ CO₂) generate the greatest total moles of gas here |

---

## 3.7 — Formation of C₄AF

C₄AF = 4CaO·Al₂O₃·Fe₂O₃ (calcium aluminoferrite)

$$\boxed{4\text{CaO} + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ca}_4\text{Al}_2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_{10}}$$

*Verification: Ca: 4=4, Al: 2=2, Fe: 2=2, O: 4+3+3 = 10 ✓*

C₃A = 3CaO·Al₂O₃. Using Ca(OH)₂ in place of CaO eliminates the CO₂-releasing calcination step. The hydrated phase is 3CaO·Al₂O₃·3H₂O:

$$\boxed{3\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow 3\text{CaO·Al}_2\text{O}_3\text{·3H}_2\text{O}}$$

*Verification: Ca: 3=3, Al: 2=2, O: 6+3=9=3+3+3 ✓, H: 6=6 ✓*

The water of hydration is supplied directly by Ca(OH)₂, bypassing the CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ decomposition and reducing CO₂ emissions.

# Problem 4: Urinary Amylase

## 4.1 — Cyclic Structure of Maltose

Maltose is **α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→4)-D-glucopyranose** — two glucose pyranose rings linked by an α-1,4-glycosidic bond. The non-reducing end has its anomeric C1 oxygen locked in the glycosidic linkage (α configuration); the reducing end retains a free anomeric C1–OH.

```
         CH₂OH                CH₂OH
          |                     |
     HO---H                HO---H
          \                    \
    HO----C         O          C----OH
    |      \      / \     O   /      |
    H       C----C   C---C--C       H
    |      /      \ /     \  \      |
    H----C         C       C  C----OH
          \       / \     /  /
           C-----C   O---C--H
          /       \     /
         H         H  OH    ← free anomeric OH (reducing end)
    
    [non-reducing glucose]──O(α-1,4)──[reducing glucose]
```

*(Both rings are α-D-glucopyranose chairs in the ⁴C₁ conformation; the glycosidic oxygen bridges C1α of the non-reducing unit to C4 of the reducing unit. The reducing end's anomeric –OH can be α or β; shown as α-α-maltose.)*

---

## 4.2

### (a) Tollen's Test — Balanced Equation

The reducing sugar (D-glucose) reacts with Tollen's reagent:

$$\underset{\text{D-Glucose}}{\text{CHO–(CHOH)}_4\text{–CH}_2\text{OH}} + 2[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+ + 3\text{OH}^- \longrightarrow \underset{\text{D-Gluconate}}{\text{COO}^-\text{–(CHOH)}_4\text{–CH}_2\text{OH}} + 2\text{Ag}(s)\downarrow + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Structures (Fischer projections):**

```
        CHO                          COO⁻
         |                            |
    H --- C --- OH               H --- C --- OH       (C2: OH right)
         |                            |
   HO --- C --- H               HO --- C --- H        (C3: OH left)
         |                            |
    H --- C --- OH               H --- C --- OH       (C4: OH right)
         |                            |
    H --- C --- OH               H --- C --- OH       (C5: OH right)
         |                            |
        CH₂OH                        CH₂OH

     D-Glucose                    D-Gluconate⁻
```

*Other reducing sugars in the mixture (maltose, oligosaccharides) also give a positive Tollen's test via their free anomeric (reducing) end.*

---

### (b) Step iv — Brownish-Black Colouration

Dipping in AgNO₃ then NaOH forms silver oxide uniformly on the plate:

$$2\text{AgNO}_3(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \longrightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) + 2\text{NaNO}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Ag₂O is **brownish-black**, coating the entire plate.

---

### (c) Step v — Disappearance of Black Colour

Thiosulfate dissolves the **unreacted** Ag₂O (regions without reducing sugars) as a soluble complex:

$$\text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) + 4\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \longrightarrow 2\text{Na}_3[\text{Ag(S}_2\text{O}_3)_2](aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq)$$

Regions where reducing sugars reduced Ag₂O to **metallic Ag** (which is insoluble in thiosulfate) retain the dark spots.

---

### (d) Reaction for the Maltose Spot

Maltose reduces Ag₂O to metallic Ag (black spot), with its reducing-end aldehyde oxidized to carboxylate:

$$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\text{ (maltose)} + \text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) \longrightarrow \text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{12}\text{ (maltobionic acid)} + 2\text{Ag}(s)$$

| Spot | Compound | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **D-Glucose** | Same high Rf as the spot in Lane 3 (U1 alone); glucose is naturally present in urine |
| **D** | **D-Glucose** | Same high Rf as the spot in Lane 4 (U2 alone) and same level as A |
| **F** | **Maltotriose** | Rf between maltose (E) and oligosaccharides (B); it is the 3-glucose-unit hydrolysis intermediate |

**Mark X for (C) and (D):**

| Statement | Verdict | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **(A)** More –OH → higher mobility | ✗ | More –OH → stronger H-bonding with silica → **lower** Rf |
| **(B)** More –OH → lower affinity with silica | ✗ | More –OH → **higher** affinity with silica (polar interactions) |
| **(C)** ↑ mobility with ↑ –OH per unit molar mass | **X** ✓ | Glucose (5 OH/180 g mol⁻¹) has highest Rf; starch (~3 OH/162 g mol⁻¹ per repeat unit) has lowest Rf. Consistent with all observed Rf values. |
| **(D)** Lower mobility of larger carbohydrates | **X** ✓ | Directly observed: glucose > maltose > maltotriose > oligosaccharides > starch in Rf |

---

## 4.3

### (a) Structures of Y and Z

**Y = 5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), C₆H₆O₃:**

```
        O
       / \
  H---C   C---CH₂OH
      ‖   |
      C   C
       \ /
        (furan ring)
```
*5-(Hydroxymethyl)furan-2-carbaldehyde — formed by acid-catalyzed dehydration of glucose by H₂SO₄.*

**Z = 2-[Bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)methyl]furan-5-carbaldehyde, C₁₈H₁₄O₄:**

```

         \              /
          C₂ -------- C₅
         / |          | \
        H  O (ring)   H
        
   furan-2-yl bears: –CH(C₆H₄OH)₂  (diaryl-CH bridge)
   furan-5-yl bears: –CHO           (aldehyde)
```

*Formed by acid-catalyzed electrophilic condensation of HMF's aldehyde with two phenol molecules at the para positions, followed by oxidation of –CH₂OH to –CHO by H₂SO₄. The extended donor–π–acceptor conjugation (phenol → furan → aldehyde) produces the orange-yellow chromophore.*

---

The reaction is the **acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of maltose** by H₂SO₄ on the TLC plate:

$$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\text{ (maltose)} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} 2\;\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\text{ (glucose)}$$

# Problem 5: A Purple Haze

---

## 5.1 — Ground-State Electronic Configuration of Iodine (Z = 53)

$$\boxed{(c)\; [\text{Kr}]\,4d^{10}\,5s^2\,5p^5}$$

Iodine is in Period 5, Group 17. The noble-gas core is [Kr] (Z = 36), with 17 remaining electrons filling 4d¹⁰, 5s², 5p⁵.

---

## Part A: Extraction of Iodine

### 5.2 — Courtois' Discovery

Seaweed ash contained sodium/potassium iodide. Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidized I⁻ to I₂:

$$2\text{NaI} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(conc.)} \longrightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{SO}_2\!\uparrow + \text{I}_2\!\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

The violet I₂ vapour condensed into shiny purplish-black crystals on the cooler vessel walls.

---

### 5.3 — Balanced Ionic Equations (Method 1)

**Step i** — Iodate reduced to iodide by bisulfite:

$$\text{IO}_3^- + 3\,\text{HSO}_3^- \longrightarrow \text{I}^- + 3\,\text{SO}_4^{2-} + 3\,\text{H}^+$$

*Check: I(+5→−1), 6e⁻ gained; S(+4→+6), 2e⁻ lost ×3 = 6e⁻ ✓*

**Step ii** — Iodide and iodate react (comproportionation):

$$\text{IO}_3^- + 5\,\text{I}^- + 6\,\text{H}^+ \longrightarrow 3\,\text{I}_2 + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

---

### 5.4 — Oxidation Numbers of Iodine Species

| Species | Formula | Oxidation state of I |
|---|---|---|
| Iodate | IO₃⁻ | **+5** |
| Iodide | I⁻ | **−1** |
| Molecular iodine | I₂ | **0** |

---

### 5.5 — Nature of Solution After Iodine Formation

Using 5/6 of concentrate for step i and 1/6 for step ii (to satisfy the 5 I⁻ : 1 IO₃⁻ stoichiometry):

- Step i produces **15 mol H⁺** (per 5 mol IO₃⁻ reduced)
- Step ii consumes **6 mol H⁺**

**Net H⁺ = 15 − 6 = 9 mol** → solution is **acidic**.

$$\boxed{(a)\;\text{acidic}}$$

---

### 5.6 — Balanced Equations for Method 2

**Step 1:** CuSO₄ + FeSO₄ + KI → white precipitate of CuI

Fe²⁺ reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu⁺ (driven by extreme insolubility of CuI, Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹²):

$$2\text{CuSO}_4 + 2\text{FeSO}_4 + 2\text{KI} \longrightarrow 2\text{CuI}\!\downarrow_{(\text{white})} + \text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 + \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$$

**Step 2:** CuI heated with K₂CO₃ → KI solution + red-brown precipitate (Cu₂O):

$$2\text{CuI} + \text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Cu}_2\text{O}\!\downarrow_{(\text{red-brown})} + 2\text{KI} + \text{CO}_2\!\uparrow$$

**Step 3:** KI solution oxidized with Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ → I₂:

$$\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 6\text{KI} + 7\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \longrightarrow 3\text{I}_2 + \text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 + 3\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

---

### 5.7 — Iodometric Titration: Reactions and Calculation

**Reaction 1** (liberation of I₂ from IO₃⁻ with excess KI in acid):

$$\text{IO}_3^- + 5\,\text{I}^- + 6\,\text{H}^+ \longrightarrow 3\,\text{I}_2 + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Reaction 2** (back-titration of I₂ with thiosulfate):

$$2\,\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} + \text{I}_2 \longrightarrow \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-} + 2\,\text{I}^-$$

**Stoichiometric chain:** 1 IO₃⁻ → 3 I₂ → 6 S₂O₃²⁻

**Calculation:**

$$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = 0.002 \times 0.0124 = 2.48 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol}$$

$$n(\text{IO}_3^-) = \frac{2.48 \times 10^{-5}}{6} = 4.133 \times 10^{-6}\text{ mol}$$

$$m(\text{I}) = 4.133 \times 10^{-6} \times 126.90 = 5.245 \times 10^{-4}\text{ g} = 0.5245\text{ mg}$$

This iodine is from **10 g of salt** (50 mL aliquot from 250 mL solution of 50 g salt).

$$\boxed{\text{Iodine content} = 0.5245 \times \frac{1000}{10} \approx 52.4\text{ mg per kg of salt}}$$

---

## Part B: Bonding and Colour of Iodine

### 5.8 — MO Shape Labels

| Shape | Description | Label |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | p-orbitals along z, out-of-phase (nodal plane) | **σ\*₅pz** |
| 2 | p-orbitals ⊥ z, in-phase side-on (px) | **π₅px** |
| 3 | p-orbitals ⊥ z, in-phase side-on (py, orthogonal to Shape 2) | **π₅py** |
| 4 | p-orbitals ⊥ z, out-of-phase side-on (px, nodal plane) | **π\*₅px** |
| 5 | s-orbitals out-of-phase (nodal plane) | **σ\*₅s** |
| 6 | p-orbitals along z, in-phase head-on | **σ₅pz** |
| 7 | s-orbitals in-phase | **σ₅s** |
| 8 | p-orbitals ⊥ z, out-of-phase side-on (py, orthogonal to Shape 4) | **π\*₅py** |

---

### 5.9 — MO Energy Level Diagram and Electron Configuration

**MO ordering** (for heavy homonuclear diatomics, analogous to O₂/F₂ ordering — minimal s–p mixing):

$$\sigma_{5s} < \sigma^*_{5s} < \sigma_{5p_z} < \pi_{5p_x} = \pi_{5p_y} < \pi^*_{5p_x} = \pi^*_{5p_y} < \sigma^*_{5p_z}$$

**14 valence electrons** (7 per iodine atom) fill the MOs:

| MO | Electrons |
|---|---|
| σ₅s | 2 |
| σ\*₅s | 2 |
| σ₅pz | 2 |
| π₅px | 2 |
| π₅py | 2 |
| π\*₅px | 2 |
| π\*₅py | 2 |
| σ\*₅pz | 0 |

$$\boxed{(\sigma_{5s})^2(\sigma^*_{5s})^2(\sigma_{5p_z})^2(\pi_{5p_x})^2(\pi_{5p_y})^2(\pi^*_{5p_x})^2(\pi^*_{5p_y})^2}$$

---

### 5.10 — Electronic Transition Responsible for Violet Colour

The violet colour arises from the **HOMO → LUMO** transition:

$$\boxed{\pi^*_{5p} \longrightarrow \sigma^*_{5p_z}}$$

- **Initial state (HOMO):** π\*₅p (degenerate filled pair)
- **Final state (LUMO):** σ\*₅pz (empty)

This transition falls in the visible region (~520 nm green absorption), transmitting violet/blue light — giving iodine vapour its characteristic colour.

---

### 5.11 — Formation of the HOMO in Triiodide (I₃⁻)

In I₃⁻, I⁻ acts as a **donor** and I₂ as an **acceptor** along the linear I–I–I axis:

| Fragment | Orbital | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **I⁻** | **5p_z AO** (HOMO of I⁻) | Electron-pair donor |
| **I₂** | **σ\*₅pz MO** (LUMO of I₂) | Electron-pair acceptor |

The filled **5p_z** orbital of I⁻ combines with the empty **σ\*₅pz** orbital of I₂ to generate the **three-center–four-electron (3c-4e)** bonding framework of I₃⁻. The resulting HOMO of I₃⁻ is the **non-bonding MO** (σ_n), with electron density localized on the two terminal iodine atoms and a node at the central atom.
